explanations.explanation: Joab, David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), gives the reason straight: "…because the king's son is dead." The battle was won, but Joab sees that the news isn't simple for a father. He tells Ahimaaz, "You may do it another day." This is a heavy part of the story, friend.

Joab never says that. His reason is that "the king's son is dead." Joab then sends a runner to tell the king what he has seen, so the fighting is not what holds Ahimaaz back. The news is just heavier than Ahimaaz thinks.

Not quite. Joab tells a Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." You don't send a runner to someone who already has the news. Joab's reason for holding Ahimaaz back is that "the king's son is dead."
The text says the opposite. Ahimaaz "persisted" and said, "No matter what, please let me also run behind the Cushite!" Joab even asks him why he'd run with no reward coming. Ahimaaz does not drop it.

Right, he does not drop it. Ahimaaz "persisted," and he asks Joab, "No matter what, please let me also run behind the Cushite!" Joab hands him a whole reason to stay put, and Ahimaaz hears none of it. I wish I had that kind of stubbornness when the oven timer goes off.

Joab says, "Then run!" Ahimaaz said "No matter what, I want to run!" and Joab gave in. I think Joab could tell arguing with him was going nowhere. Sometimes the answer is yes just to get a man to stop asking.
Joab never says that. Ahimaaz says, "No matter what, I want to run!" and Joab answers, "Then run!" The commander lets him go.
Joab sends him nowhere near the troops. After Ahimaaz insists, Joab tells him, "Then run!" So Ahimaaz takes off, with the message and all.
The text says Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." The Cushite had the head start and still lost the race. Starting behind and finishing in front is a good feeling, friend.
It's the other way around. The Cushite took off first, but Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." Ahimaaz is the one who wins this race.
No waiting happens here. Ahimaaz "ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite." He passes the Cushite instead of standing around for him.
David says, "If he is alone, he bears good news." A lone runner means good news to the king. He's reading the situation from the sound of one set of feet.
David says the opposite. His words are, "If he is alone, he bears good news." A man running alone doesn't mean the battle is lost to David.
David doesn't say that. He tells the watchman, "If he is alone, he bears good news." The man running alone is a sign of good news to the king.
The watchman calls out about another man running alone, and the king says, "This one also brings good news." David uses the same rule again. A lone runner still means good news to him.
David actually says, "This one also brings good news." The watchman spotted another man running alone, and the king gave the same answer as before. It's true, friend.

The watchman says the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok. David answers, "This is a good man. He comes with good news." Ahimaaz is Zadok's son, and David speaks well of him before he even arrives.
It's true. David hears the watchman say the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok, and he says, "This is a good man. He comes with good news." David is speaking kindly about Ahimaaz.

David asks, "Is the young man Absalom all right?" Absalom is David's son, the one who rose up against him. Ahimaaz brought news of victory, and the king asks about his son first. I think that tells you where his heart is.
David doesn't ask about Joab. He asks, "Is the young man Absalom all right?" Absalom is David's son, and the question about him comes right after the news of the win.
David never asks that. After hearing the news of the win, he asks, "Is the young man Absalom all right?" His question is about his son.
Joab did say the king's son is dead, but Ahimaaz doesn't tell David that. He says, "I saw a great tumult, but I do not know what it was." So David hears no word of Absalom's death from him.

Ahimaaz tells David, "I saw a great tumult, but I do not know what it was." He doesn't say the king's son is dead, though Joab told him so (2 Samuel 18:20). David asked about Absalom, and Ahimaaz gave him no answer.
David asks the Cushite the same question: "Is the young man Absalom all right?" Those are the exact words he asked Ahimaaz earlier. David wants to know about his son.
The question is the same. The king asks the Cushite, "Is the young man Absalom all right?" He asked Ahimaaz those same words. The Cushite answers it where Ahimaaz didn't.

The Cushite never says the word, but his wish makes it plain: "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man." Joab already said the king's son is dead (2 Samuel 18:20). David understands the answer.
An escape doesn't fit what the Cushite says. He wishes David's enemies would "be like that young man." Joab had already said the king's son is dead (2 Samuel 18:20).

The Cushite doesn't say this. He wishes David's enemies would "be like that young man." Joab had already said the king's son is dead (2 Samuel 18:20), and the Cushite answers David's question about Absalom with that wish.
The text says the king "went up to the chamber over the gate and wept." He was already sitting at the gate when the news came. He goes up to weep there.
David doesn't go there to weep. The text says he "went up to the chamber over the gate and wept." He stays by the gate where he had been waiting.
The forest is where the battle was fought, and David isn't there. The text says he "went up to the chamber over the gate and wept." He weeps right by the gate where he waited for news.
David cries, "If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!" This is a father's grief, and it's heavy. He says it over and over.
David doesn't say that. He cries, "If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!" That wish comes straight out of his grief.
David says nothing about fleeing here. He cries, "If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!" It's a father's heartbreak.
The text says, "And that day's victory was turned into mourning for all the people." They were told, "The king is grieving over his son." The whole mood of the day turns around.

The word is not fear. The text says, "that day's victory was turned into mourning for all the people." The people were told, "The king is grieving over his son."
The text says, "the king covered his face and cried out at the top of his voice." He is crying out his son's name, again and again. The people hear about it, and so does Joab.
It's true. "The king covered his face and cried out at the top of his voice," the text says. David is still grieving his son, even after the people have come back.
Joab says, "You love those who hate you and hate those who love you!" Those are Joab's words to the king, and they're blunt. He says them to David face to face.

explanations.answer: Go out and comfort his servants
explanations.explanation: Joab says, "Now therefore get up! Go out and speak comfort to your servants." He wants David to go out to his men. Joab doesn't hold back.

explanations.answer: Stay inside until the mourning ends
explanations.explanation: Joab says the opposite. He tells David, "Get up! Go out and speak comfort to your servants." He wants the king out of the house.

explanations.answer: Go out and bury Absalom himself
explanations.explanation: Joab says nothing about burying anyone. He tells David, "Get up! Go out and speak comfort to your servants." Joab's focus is the men.
Joab swears by the LORD, but not about half. He says, "…if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight." Half would be a lot less than that. Joab means every last man.
Joab says, "…I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight." Not half, but not a man. Joab doesn't go easy on the king.
The text says the people were told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." Then "they all came before the king." David has gotten up as Joab urged.
It's true. The people were told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate," and "they all came before the king." The king is out where his men can see him.
